No per-container or per-CWT container rate is stated on this page. Does this page cover reefer, bonded, or customs work? No. Reefer and cold-chain handling, bonded warehouse or foreign-trade zone operation, and customs brokerage are not claimed on this page. Container jobs are quoted per job — send the job details through Get My Flat Rate Quote . What if the load includes a very heavy item? If a transload involves a high-mass asset in the 1,500–3,500 lb range, that asset moves under Structural Integrity Relocation (SIR), with floor deflection analysis to L/360, as part of the same flat-rate job. SIR is not claimed for transloading generally; it applies only where such an asset is actually involved. How do I get a flat rate quote for a transload? answerFragments.locator: Transloading Services — Winchester VA. › What transloading is
answerFragments.heading: What transloading is
answerFragments.text: What transloading is Transloading is unloading plus immediate reload into domestic equipment: typically a 40ft ocean container's cargo restacked into 53ft domestic trailers, so the ocean box returns near the port and the domestic trailer carries the inland leg. It gives the shipper control over routing, speed to multiple markets, and capacity use. The words around it, as the industry uses them: Unloading (devanning / destuffing) — removing cargo from an ocean container at a warehouse or container freight station, then sorting and staging it for delivery. "Destuffing" is the same operation; the word is standard on Asian and UK trade documents. Cross-docking — freight that never enters storage: it touches the dock floor for hours, not days, then leaves on outbound LTL or FTL the same shift. A transload is often done as a cross-dock move, but it can also include a few days of storage between legs. Deconsolidation (decon) — breaking a consolidated container apart by destination, purchase order, or SKU: the step that turns one inbound box into many outbound loads. Drayage — the short-range move, usually 100 miles or less, that carries a released container from its port of arrival to a nearby warehouse or storage facility. It is a step in the chain described below; this page does not state who performs it (see Questions, answered). IPI vs transload — under IPI (inland point intermodal), the original ocean container continues inland to the destination. Under transloading, cargo transfers to domestic equipment in the first mile, which adds control and visibility and makes it easier to pivot between rail and truck.

answerFragments.locator: Transloading Services — Winchester VA. › How a transload runs
answerFragments.heading: How a transload runs
answerFragments.text: How a transload runs The chain, step by step, with the company's verified steps in it: 1. Pre-arrival planning — outbound routing, destination addresses, load plan, and equipment count confirmed before the vessel arrives; the transload appointment booked before the container leaves the terminal. 2. Port release and the short move in — the container is picked up at the terminal as soon as it is released and delivered to the transload and warehouse facility inside the ocean carrier's free time. 3. Devanning, count, and inspection — the container is unloaded, floor-loaded or palletized; freight is counted and inspected; damage is photographed and reported the same day, in writing, so the buyer sees actual cargo condition before it travels inland. 4. Rework — cargo is palletized if needed, shrink-wrapped, labeled, sorted by purchase order, SKU, or destination, and segregated for multi-destination loads. 5. Restacking into domestic equipment — cargo is restacked into 53ft trailers (a 40ft container becomes about 20 pallet positions; a 20ft about 10) or staged for storage. 6. Inland dispatch — trailers depart same-day or next-morning for warehouses, distribution centers, retail partners, or final customers, as FTL, LTL, or split delivery. 7. Empty return — the ocean container returns to the terminal immediately after devanning, before per-diem charges start. 8. Final mile — last-leg delivery to stores, offices, homes, and job sites by appointment, through the company's verified final-mile delivery service. The company's own published steps sit inside this chain: receive, unload, count, sort by destination, stage, and build outbound (container deconsolidation reference), and quoted, surveyed, packed, loaded, transloaded, delivered, and verified placement (logistics event protocol).

answerFragments.locator: Transloading Services — Winchester VA. › The cost-avoidance terms
answerFragments.heading: The cost-avoidance terms
answerFragments.text: The cost-avoidance terms These are industry terms, stated here as domain facts — they are the reason transload speed matters: Free time and last free day (LFD) — every container has free time at the terminal and with the carrier. Past the last free day, charges start. Demurrage — the charge for a box sitting at the terminal past free time. Detention (per-diem) — the charge for a box kept outside the terminal past free time. Chassis — the wheeled frame a container rides on for the short move. Chassis sourcing, shortages, and tri-axle chassis for overweight boxes are routine cost and schedule variables. The overweight alternative — where a container genuinely cannot be permitted to destination, transloading its cargo into domestic trailers removes the container weight from the equation; for some lanes that is cheaper than permitting even when a permit is available. Moving a box inside free time is the entire cost-avoidance game. Warehouse storage is cheaper than port demurrage, which is why importers use the short move to a warehouse when congestion makes long-range scheduling unreliable.

answerFragments.locator: 3PL & Project Support at the Virginia Inland Port › The terminal, and the cluster around it
answerFragments.heading: The terminal, and the cluster around it
answerFragments.text: The terminal, and the cluster around it The Virginia Inland Port (7685 Winchester Road, Front Royal, VA 22630) is the Virginia Port Authority's inland intermodal terminal: about 160 acres, design capacity of 78,000 TEUs, 17,820 feet of rail track, 24 reefer plugs, and on-site log stuffing, opened in 1989. Containers transfer between Norfolk Southern rail and truck under steamship bill of lading — rail is the long-haul leg to and from the Norfolk Harbor terminals, truck is the last-mile leg into Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania. The terminal is a U.S. Customs-designated port of entry, its gate runs Monday–Friday 0700–1600, and it sits within a mile of I-66 on the US-340/522 corridor. The designated federal foreign-trade-zone site at Front Royal is FTZ 20 Site 7 — the Warren County Industrial Corridor, grantee Virginia Port Authority. Around the terminal, the Front Royal–Warren County EDA lists UPS, Family Dollar, Ferguson and Sysco distribution hubs in Front Royal and Warren County, with Axalta Coating Systems and Toray Plastics (America) within two miles. That cluster — national distribution, parcel, foodservice and industrial operations on one corridor — is the buyer set this service exists for. Naming them is geography, not a client claim: they are the EDA's published picture of who operates here, and the offer on this page is addressed to operations like them.

answerFragments.locator: 3PL & Project Support at the Virginia Inland Port › Questions, answered
answerFragments.heading: Questions, answered
answerFragments.text: Questions, answered What is 3PL support, exactly? It is the crew layer a 3PL, distribution center or carrier brings in for defined work — receiving and devanning containers, sorting and segregating freight, cross-dock turns, rework and surge labor — executed by our supervised crews to a written plan. We support the operation; we do not become the operator. Who hires this service at the Virginia Inland Port? 3PL site managers, distribution-center managers, carriers and receivers with container flow through the Front Royal terminal — typically for a surge, a backlog, a project, or a start-up their standing labor cannot absorb. Where does the work take place? At port-adjacent warehouses, receivers' docks, yards and leased space around Front Royal and the Winchester corridor. On-terminal work happens only by arrangement through the terminal's own processes. Do you run drayage to and from the port? No. Drayage is not part of this service. Freight moves on your trucks or your carrier's trucks; our work is the hands-on layer at the delivery point. How is it priced? Every engagement is surveyed and scoped in full, then quoted at one flat rate — scope, distance, manpower and equipment reviewed and agreed before dispatch. Hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it. Are your crews credentialed for port work? Our crews hold TWIC cards and our contractors hold valid TWIC cards. That is card-holding by the people doing the work — the company claims no port tenancy and no port-authority relationship.

answerFragments.locator: Virginia Inland Port transloading — the floor behind the ramp. › The port itself
answerFragments.heading: The port itself
answerFragments.text: The port itself The Virginia Inland Port — 7685 Winchester Road, Front Royal, VA 22630 — is owned and operated by the Virginia Port Authority , with day-to-day terminal operation by Virginia International Terminals. It opened in 1989 as the Commonwealth's inland intermodal terminal: a dry port where containers transfer between Norfolk Southern rail and truck under steamship bill of lading. Rail is the long-haul leg to and from the Norfolk Harbor terminals (Norfolk International Terminals and Virginia International Gateway); truck is the last-mile leg into Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania. Because rail weight limits are less restrictive than road limits, higher-weighted containers can move through here that could not legally run the whole way by truck. The terminal is a U.S. Customs-designated port of entry with the full range of Customs functions, and its gate runs Monday–Friday, 0700–1600 . It sits on the US-340/522 (Winchester Road) corridor, within a mile of I-66, adjacent to Norfolk Southern's Crescent Corridor main line — the rail line that parallels I-81 through the Valley. The designated federal foreign-trade-zone site at Front Royal is FTZ 20 Site 7 — the Warren County Industrial Corridor (490 acres, Routes 340/522/661), grantee Virginia Port Authority. (Warren County also falls inside FTZ 185's service area ; a service area is not a site designation, and FTZ 185's grantee is the County of Culpeper — the distinction is recorded in the estate's ports dataset because the error circulates widely.) The port's customs and FTZ statuses belong to the port; what this company adds is the hands-on layer around the freight that moves through it.

answerFragments.locator: Virginia Inland Port transloading — the floor behind the ramp. › The words, defined
answerFragments.heading: The words, defined
answerFragments.text: The words, defined Transloading Unloading freight from one mode or unit and reloading it into another — here, out of an ocean container and into domestic trailers, trucks or staged warehouse positions — so the ocean box turns back and the freight continues inland in the equipment the inland leg runs best in. Deconsolidation Breaking one consolidated container into many outbound loads, sorted by destination, order, SKU, store, site or region. One box in, many deliveries out. Cross-docking The freight never enters storage: it crosses the dock from inbound to outbound the same turn. If it waits for a timed release instead, that is staging — a defined state, not a default. Devanning Unloading an ocean container at a warehouse floor rather than at the vessel terminal — also called destuffing on many trade documents. Floor-loaded freight comes out piece by piece; palletized freight is pulled by forklift. Rework The work a load needs before it can move again: repalletizing onto sound pallets, rewrapping in stretch wrap, bracing and banding, relabeling — and, for open-deck freight, tarping or re-tarping. Damaged or shifted loads are reported and reworked on the floor, not passed on. Tarping & re-tarping Covering open-deck freight — flatbed, step-deck and similar trailers that give cargo no protection from rain, snow, wind or debris — with heavy tarps secured by bungee cords, rope or straps. Re-tarping is replacing or re-securing a tarp that has loosened, torn or shifted in transit, so the load is weather-tight again. On our floor it is a rework step inside a transloading or recovery job, never a standalone service.

answerFragments.locator: Virginia Inland Port transloading — the floor behind the ramp. › How a container moves through the floor
answerFragments.heading: How a container moves through the floor
answerFragments.text: How a container moves through the floor Step What happens 1 · Arrival The container reaches the corridor by Norfolk Southern rail through the inland port ramp, or by truck on I-81, I-66 or I-70. The turn is planned as a scheduled operation inside the carrier’s free time — an unplanned queue at the door is where demurrage and detention clocks start. 2 · Seal & paperwork The seal number is checked against the shipping documents before the container is opened. Short counts, seal mismatches and damage are documented at intake, not discovered at delivery. 3 · Devanning Floor-loaded freight is unloaded piece by piece; palletized freight is pulled by forklift. Everything is counted against the paperwork and checked as it crosses the dock. 4 · Deconsolidation The container is split into outbound loads sorted by destination, order, SKU, store, site or region. 5 · Cross-dock or stage Straight-through freight passes inbound to outbound without storage. Freight held for timed release is staged by destination until its window. 6 · Rework Where a load needs it: repalletizing onto sound pallets, rewrapping in stretch wrap, bracing and banding, relabeling — and tarping or re-tarping open-deck freight so the onward leg leaves weather-tight. Salvageable freight is separated, counted and restacked; damaged freight is set aside and reported as found. 7 · Outbound build Loads are built into 53 ft domestic trailers — three 40 ft ocean containers of light, floor-loaded freight typically consolidate into two 53 ft trailers — or into less-than-truckload and full-truckload runs, or handed to final-mile delivery with placement. 8 · Empty turn The empty container is turned around instead of sitting, closing the free-time loop. 9 · Export, in reverse Outbound freight is received, packed and braced, crated to ISPM 15 where the shipment needs it, and loaded for the port leg through the inland port to Hampton Roads.

answerFragments.locator: Virginia Inland Port transloading — the floor behind the ramp. › Load rework — and where tarping fits
answerFragments.heading: Load rework — and where tarping fits
answerFragments.text: Load rework — and where tarping fits A load that arrives shifted, collapsed, water-damaged or refused cannot simply be sent on. Recovery work separates what is salvageable, counts and restacks it, and sets damaged freight aside, reported as found. Open-deck freight adds one more failure mode: a tarp that loosened, tore or shifted leaves the load open to the weather, and carriers will not move it until it is covered and secured again. That re-covering — re-tarping — is part of rework on our floor, alongside repalletizing, rewrapping, bracing and relabeling. The materials the work consumes — tarps and tie-downs, stretch wrap, pallets, banding, labels and markers — are purchased for each project and scoped inside the job’s one flat rate. What tarping costs in the wider market is published by the carriers themselves. Anderson Trucking Service’s tarping guide puts a driver-applied tarp at $50 to $150 for a legal load, a $200 to $300 over-dimensional tarp charge, and up to $750 or more on heavy-haul freight. Those are carrier accessorial figures for open-deck trailers — market data, shown so you can recognize the line on a freight bill. They are not our prices: rework on our floor is scoped and priced inside the one flat rate quoted for your job, in writing, before dispatch. Carrier market reference (ATS) Published figure Tarping a legal load $50–$150 Over-dimensional tarp charge $200–$300 Heavy-haul tarping (freight over 14 ft 6 in wide, 14 ft 6 in high, or 100 ft long) Up to $750 or more Drop tarps Tarps with hanging side flaps sized by their drop — 4 ft, 6 ft and 8 ft drops are common — typically 20 to 24 ft long. The pair a driver carries covers most freight. Steel tarps Rectangular tarps with no drops, commonly about 20 by 20 ft or 20 by 26 ft; they can overlap to cover odd-shaped loads. Smoke tarp A smaller tarp protecting the front of a load from exhaust soot. Heavy tarps weigh around 100 lb, which is why applying them is priced as premium work in the carrier market — and why a load that needs re-covering belongs on a floor with a crew, not on a shoulder.

A shifted, collapsed or refused load is recovered on the floor: salvageable freight is separated, counted and restacked, damaged freight is set aside and reported as found, and the rebuilt load is repalletized, rewrapped in stretch wrap, braced and banded before it moves. Open-deck freight is tarped or re-tarped in the same rework, so the onward leg leaves weather-tight.

answerFragments.heading: What does tarping or re-tarping a load involve, and what does it cost?
answerFragments.text: What does tarping or re-tarping a load involve, and what does it cost? Tarping covers open-deck freight — flatbed, step-deck and similar trailers that give cargo no protection from rain, snow, wind or debris — with heavy tarps secured by bungee cords, rope or straps. Re-tarping replaces or re-secures a tarp that has loosened, torn or shifted in transit. In the carrier market, Anderson Trucking Service publishes $50 to $150 to tarp a legal load, $200 to $300 for an over-dimensional tarp charge, and up to $750 or more for heavy-haul tarping — those are carrier accessorial figures, not our prices. On our floor, tarping and re-tarping are rework steps scoped inside the job's one flat rate, quoted in writing before dispatch.

answerFragments.locator: FAQ schema (per-page JSON FAQPage)
answerFragments.heading: Do you offer bonded warehousing, customs brokerage or FTZ services?
answerFragments.text: Do you offer bonded warehousing, customs brokerage or FTZ services? No — and the distinction matters. The Virginia Inland Port is a U.S. Customs-designated port of entry, and its ground in the Warren County Industrial Corridor is covered by Foreign Trade Zone 20 magnet sites (the zone’s grantee is the Virginia Port Authority); Warren County also lies within Foreign Trade Zone 185’s service area, which is not a site designation. Those are the port's statuses, not ours. We are a private handling operation near the port: we do not broker customs, we operate no bonded warehouse and no foreign-trade zone activity, and we claim no refrigerated or cold-chain handling and no hazmat handling. What we do is the physical work — unload, count, split, stage, rework and deliver the freight.

answerFragments.text: How fast can a container be turned once it reaches the Valley? Turns are planned as scheduled operations inside the carrier's free time, because that clock — not the unload itself — is where container costs are won or lost. The exact timing for your container is set in the written quote, from the freight detail you give us: container size, floor-loaded or palletized, piece count, destination and timing. Empties are turned around instead of sitting.

answerFragments.locator: Warehouse Racking Relocation — Winchester VA & Martinsburg WV › Racking relocation, explained — industry background, not our terms › The standard the work is held to
answerFragments.heading: The standard the work is held to
answerFragments.text: The standard the work is held to Industrial steel storage racks in the United States are governed by ANSI MH16.1, the Rack Manufacturers Institute (RMI) specification for the design, testing and utilization of industrial steel storage racks — current edition MH16.1-2023 — referenced by the International Building Code. Its installation requirements include: every column base-plated and anchored, with anchor type, size and torque set by the project's sealed Load Application and Rack Configuration (LARC) drawings; a maximum out-of-plumb of 1/240 top to bottom for a loaded rack; height-to-depth stability limits; and load plaques posted on the rack showing maximum unit load, average unit load, and maximum total load per bay. Cantilever racks sit under a companion standard, ANSI MH16.3, and rack decking under ANSI MH26.2. OSHA publishes no dedicated rack standard: warehouse work runs under the federal materials-handling and powered-industrial-truck rules (29 CFR 1910.176 and 1910.178), and OSHA recognizes MH16.1 as the consensus standard when it cites rack hazards under the General Duty Clause.

answerFragments.heading: Questions, answered
answerFragments.text: Questions, answered Who disassembles and reassembles pallet racking when a warehouse moves? In this corridor, we do — as one job with the move itself. The Flat Rate Movers tears down pallet racking, moves the inventory that was on it, transports steel and product together, stages both in storage if the destination is not ready, and reinstalls the racking level, plumb and anchored at the new building. It is the combination the market splits across dealers, installers and movers: teardown, transport, inventory and reinstall under one flat rate, from Winchester VA and Martinsburg WV. How much does it cost to relocate pallet racking? Each job is priced at one flat rate in writing after a survey of the full scope — bay count, beam levels, upright heights, what is on the steel, distance, phasing, and whether staging is needed. There is no per-bay rate card and no published hourly price. For budget structure, the published market figures are in "Racking relocation, explained" above: installers publish labor at $20 to $50 per pallet position and $150 to $400 per bay, and relocating a system typically runs 30 to 50 percent of buying it new. Those are industry figures, not our prices — our price for your job is the written flat rate for your job. Can I reuse my existing racking in a new warehouse, or should I buy new? Reuse is usually the right economics — typically 30 to 50 percent of new — when three checks pass: the uprights are sound (bent or damaged components are excluded and replaced, never re-erected), the system fits the destination (heights against ceiling and sprinkler clearance, bays against the column grid, confirmed on engineered drawings before teardown), and the configuration still matches your inventory. The survey answers all three before you commit. Do you provide the engineering and permits for the reinstall? Yes — arranged inside the engagement. We hold no engineering license ourselves: rack engineering, seismic calculation and the permit application are performed by the certified contractors we consult and engage, and the local authority having jurisdiction issues the approval against their sealed drawings. Our crews perform the physical work — teardown, transport, reinstallation and anchoring to the floor — to the manufacturer's specification and ANSI MH16.1 / RMI guidance, against the project's engineered drawings and permits, with anchor type, size and torque set by the project's LARC drawings. One engagement, one flat rate: the engineering layer is handled for you, not handed back to you. What happens to damaged racking you find during teardown? It is set aside, reported to you in writing, and accounted for at closeout. Bent or damaged uprights are never re-erected — a damaged frame under load is how racks fail. Replacement components are your purchase through your dealer or engineer of record; their cost is never folded silently into the flat rate. Can you hold the racking and inventory between buildings? Yes. Storage staging is part of the service: racking and inventory held in leased storage space when the destination is not ready — 30-day minimum, with customer access — priced per job, monthly, or by volume. It is the gap in most warehouse moves, and it is why the steel and the inventory in this service travel with the same company that stores them. Do you also move the inventory, or only the steel? Both, in sequence. Inventory is pulled, palletized, wrapped and counted before the steel moves, and put back on the racking at the destination in the order your restart needs it, with counts reconciled at closeout. Moving the steel without the inventory — or the inventory without the steel — is the split this service exists to end. What about cubicles and office systems? The same discipline, office side: cubicle and systems-furniture teardown, transport and reassembly for office moves, renovations and reconfigurations — panels, worksurfaces, overhead storage and pedestals. Licensed-trade electrical and building data work stays with your contractor's trades; the furniture work is ours. How is the flat rate set? We review the full scope of each job — the work, the distance, the manpower, and the equipment — and give a flat rate, as opposed to an hourly rate. What the survey finds (tall systems, phased cutovers, staging days, a hot aisle of damaged uprights) is inside the price, not added on the day. Can contractors or rack dealers hire your crews for the teardown and reinstall labor? Yes — through Industrial & Commercial Project Support and Specialized Workforce Labor: trained, supervised, self-managed teams deployed per job, with the published per-hundredweight and per-man schedule that belongs to that workforce service. That schedule prices workforce engagements; a full racking relocation quoted to the building owner is priced per job at one flat rate.

The question that starts most of these searches has a published answer: relocating existing racking typically costs 30 to 50 percent of the price of a new system (Zhengda Rack, a rack dealer that publishes its relocation economics). A sound system is worth moving. Three things decide whether yours is sound, and all three are answered at the survey, before you are committed: the condition of the uprights (bent or impact-damaged frames do not go back up — replacement components are bought at the destination, through your dealer, and their cost is never folded silently into our rate); whether the system fits the destination (upright heights against the new ceiling and sprinkler clearance, bay widths against the new column grid — a layout confirmed on the project's engineered drawings before teardown); and whether the configuration still matches the inventory (beam levels and lane depths set for the product you store now, not the product you stored in 2019). If reuse fails any of the three, the honest job is a partial one: move what is sound, decommission the rest, and let your dealer price the difference as new steel.

answerFragments.locator: When an item needs a custom crate and when padding is enough › When is padding enough?
answerFragments.heading: When is padding enough?
answerFragments.text: When is padding enough? Padding earns its keep when the threat list is short — it handles abrasion and minor impact, and nothing more: it cannot carry a load stacked on it, stop a puncture, or fix a piece against a shifting load. Our published protection model starts every piece the same way — wrapped first, white-glove wrapping for antiques, art, instruments and fragile pieces, padding at every contact point (7). That layer, plus blankets and stretch wrap, is the complete answer when: The piece is sturdily built and its exposure is surface-level — scratches and scuffs. One crew carries it once, in one truck — no terminal, no stacking, no second carrier. uShip's own contrast is a local sofa: shrink wrap and padding (2). The destination is a room, not a warehouse shelf — placed the same day. The honest middle exists too: a standard mirror travels in a mirror carton, and medium-value fragile furniture can be double-boxed where a crate is recommended but not required (3). The line: would a failure be a scuff — or a fracture?

answerFragments.locator: When an item needs a custom crate and when padding is enough › Does an export crate play by different rules?
answerFragments.heading: Does an export crate play by different rules?
answerFragments.text: Does an export crate play by different rules? Yes — the wood becomes part of the regulation. ISPM 15 (International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15) governs solid wood packaging in international trade. As administered in the United States, heat treatment means the wood core reaches a minimum of 56 degrees Celsius for at least 30 minutes (4, 5). USDA APHIS describes the compliant routes: build from previously heat-treated lumber carrying an accredited agency mark, or heat-treat the finished packaging and apply the mark (4). Three practical consequences: The treatment codes are specific. Approved treatments include heat treatment (HT), methyl bromide fumigation (MB), sulfuryl fluoride fumigation (SF) and dielectric heating (DH); pressure-treated lumber does not qualify unless heat-treated and stamped first (5). Some materials are exempt by construction. Plywood, oriented strand board, particleboard, flakeboard and veneer sit outside the requirement — their manufacture already involves high heat — as does wood 6 mm or thinner (5). A crate's solid-wood frame and skids are not exempt; they are the regulated part. Non-compliance lands on the shipper. Our published export pages state it directly: wood packaging that does not comply can be delayed, treated at the shipper's cost, or refused (7). Our practice matches: export crates are built to ISPM 15 from compliant, heat-treated, marked wood (7). Example (illustrative): an antique marble-top sideboard is sold from a Valley estate to a buyer overseas. The piece is surveyed and measured; the marble and carved frame are wrapped first; a crate is built around it — around its weight, fragile points and center of mass — its interior blocked, braced and cushioned so nothing can shift. Because the shipment crosses a border, the crate's solid wood is compliant, heat-treated and marked. The closed crate travels the export chain — I-81 south, I-64 east to the Port of Virginia's Hampton Roads terminals — inside the one flat rate quoted for the job.

answerFragments.locator: When an item needs a custom crate and when padding is enough › Frequently asked questions
answerFragments.heading: Frequently asked questions
answerFragments.text: Frequently asked questions What is custom crating? Building a rigid wooden crate around one specific item, measured to that item, with the piece secured inside by blocking, bracing and cushioning so it cannot shift in transit (7). Packing wraps an item in flexible protection; a crate gives it a rigid shell freight systems can stack and forklift (1, 2). How much does custom crating cost? Published third-party guides put custom crating at roughly $150 to $1,000 or more per crate, against $5 to $50 for boxes and specialty cartons, with size, materials and complexity driving the figure (3). We publish no per-crate price: crating is scoped per job and quoted inside the one flat rate in writing (7). Can a custom crate be reused? Often, yes. This Old House notes that many custom-built crates are reusable, spreading the build cost across future moves (1). Whether a crate suits a second journey depends on its construction and the next piece — reuse is settled when the next job is scoped, not assumed. Does an export crate need heat-treated wood? For its solid wood components, yes. ISPM 15 requires solid wood packaging in international trade to be treated — heat treatment: a core temperature of at least 56 degrees Celsius held for 30 minutes — and marked (4, 5). Plywood and oriented strand board are exempt (5). Our export crates are built to ISPM 15 from compliant, heat-treated, marked wood (7). What is the difference between a crate, a pallet and a skid? A skid is a base — runners that carry a load and let a forklift underneath; a pallet is a flat deck on the same principle. Neither has walls. A crate is the base plus an enclosure: panels and a lid that turn protection from a platform into a structure, its interior fitted so the piece cannot shift (7). How long does it take to build a custom crate? The build follows the survey: the piece is measured, the crate designed to its weight, fragile points and center of mass, the item wrapped, and only then is the wood closed around it (7). The sequence is scheduled when the job is scoped, ahead of move day. We publish no fixed lead time.

answerFragments.text: When an item needs a custom crate and when padding is enough By Henry Pitts Jr. · Published October 31, 2026, 4:35 AM EDT Padding protects a surface; a crate protects a structure. If a piece can be crushed, punctured, stacked on or shifted against — or if it is crossing an ocean — it needs a crate. answerFragments.locator: When an item needs a custom crate and when padding is enough › When does a piece need a crate?
answerFragments.heading: When does a piece need a crate?
answerFragments.text: When does a piece need a crate? Five triggers, and any one of them settles the question: 1. The structure is the fragile part. Thin glass, stone tops, delicate carvings and fine finishes fracture under stress padding cannot absorb — the pieces guides list as crating-required, not optional (3). 2. The journey has hand-offs. Freight transferred between vehicles or terminals is forklifted and stacked at every touch. uShip's crating guide is blunt: for less-than-truckload freight, crating is not just helpful, it is expected — the crate absorbs the impacts of repeated handling (2). 3. The shape defeats padding. Oversized or irregular pieces cannot be anchored with straps and pads alone; carriers insist on a frame around them (3). 4. The piece is crossing a border. International legs add handling, humidity and long transit — and the crate's wood itself becomes regulated (3, 4). 5. The piece is going into storage. Months in a warehouse mean stacking pressure and contact from other freight; a wrapped piece takes those knocks directly (3). Value sharpens every trigger — a piece worth far more than it weighs is the classic case (3).

answerFragments.locator: Transloading at the Virginia Inland Port: the support layer behind the rail ramps › The shape of the working day at a dry port
answerFragments.heading: The shape of the working day at a dry port
answerFragments.text: The shape of the working day at a dry port The terminal sets the rhythm. The Virginia Inland Port's gate runs Monday to Friday, 0700 to 1600, so the support layer plans around a five-day, nine-hour window: containers grounded in the morning are devanned the same day wherever the delivery point allows, and empties go back before per-diem charges start to run. The terminal's facts shape the work in other ways, too. At about 160 acres with a design capacity of 78,000 TEUs, 17,820 feet of rail track and 24 reefer plugs, it is a transfer facility, not a storage port — freight is meant to keep moving, and the floor work is sequenced to that intent. On-site log stuffing serves the Valley's timber exporters; the port is a U.S. Customs-designated port of entry; and because rail weight limits are less restrictive than road limits, heavier containers can legally arrive here that could not have run the full distance by truck — one reason the freight that comes off the rail at Front Royal skews heavy and awkward, and why the crews who handle it are riggers and warehouse hands both. The designated foreign-trade-zone site at Front Royal is FTZ 20 Site 7 — the Warren County Industrial Corridor, grantee Virginia Port Authority. (The "FTZ 185" label attached to this area in many directories is an error: 185's grantee is the County of Culpeper, and Warren County lies in its service area, which is not a site designation. The estate's ports dataset records the correction with its federal sources.)

answerFragments.locator: Transloading at the Virginia Inland Port: the support layer behind the rail ramps › The ramps are the railroad's; the floor work is not
answerFragments.heading: The ramps are the railroad's; the floor work is not
answerFragments.text: The ramps are the railroad's; the floor work is not An inland port looks, from the road, like a parking lot full of containers and a rail line. That view hides the division of labor that makes the place work. The Virginia Inland Port (7685 Winchester Road, Front Royal, VA 22630) is the Virginia Port Authority's inland intermodal terminal, opened in 1989, with day-to-day operation by Virginia International Terminals. Its job is the transfer: containers arrive and depart by Norfolk Southern rail — the terminal sits adjacent to the NS Crescent Corridor main line — and leave or arrive by truck under steamship bill of lading. Rail is the long-haul leg to and from Norfolk International Terminals and Virginia International Gateway on Hampton Roads; truck is the last-mile leg into Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania. None of that touches the freight. A container that comes off the rail at Front Royal still has to be opened, unloaded, counted against its paperwork, sorted, restacked and loaded into domestic equipment — or held, reworked, or turned back out the gate. That work does not happen on the ramp. It happens at the port-adjacent warehouses, receivers' docks, yards and leased space around the terminal, and it is done by whoever the freight's owner, carrier or 3PL puts on the floor. That is the support layer, and it is where a transload succeeds or fails: the mode change is the terminal's; the freight change is the crew's.

answerFragments.heading: The five jobs of the support layer
answerFragments.text: The five jobs of the support layer Receive and devan. The container is received at the door, the seal checked, the doors opened and the load unloaded — floor-loaded or palletized, in a sequence that keeps freight stable and countable. Doors, seal, condition and load are photographed before the first case moves, because the devanning record is the last clean look at the freight before inland travel. Count and report. Every case is counted against the packing paperwork as it comes off, not after the container is empty. Exceptions — damage, shortage, overage — are reported the same day, in writing, while the evidence is still on the floor. Damage caught at devanning is damage caught before it becomes a claim argument three states away. Sort and segregate. One container rarely belongs to one destination. Freight is deconsolidated by destination, purchase order or SKU as it is unloaded, so the fan-out is built during the devan rather than reconstructed afterwards. Restack and reload. Sorted freight is built into outbound loads — palletized, wrapped, and loaded into the 53-foot domestic trailer, the LTL shipment, or the split delivery — or crossed straight through in a cross-dock turn with dwell measured in hours. Rework the exceptions. Shifted loads are corrected, crushed cases segregated, pallets rebuilt, labels replaced. A load that arrives wrong leaves right, and the refused-delivery phone call never happens. That is the whole craft: five jobs, done in order, with a written record. It is skilled, unglamorous, and — as anyone who has searched for it around Front Royal knows — remarkably hard to find a named provider for. The money phrases tell the story: "transloading near Virginia Inland Port" had no Front Royal holder at all when this estate last measured the field. The ramps have an operator. The support layer, until now, has had nobody's name on it.

gapRecords.impact: No console exists for ChatGPT / Claude / Perplexity citation standing; zero panel observations have ever been run. Every other gap in this element is ranked on supply-side reasoning because the outcome measure does not exist.
gapRecords.status: instrument built; first runs ingested 2026-11-01 and 2026-11-02 (33 rows); monthly cadence booked
gapRecords.resolvingBatch: Element 2 build batch B2 (Answer Panel instrument + first run)
gapRecords.solution: The Answer Panel: a fixed panel of money questions generated from the rubric (panel set membership is a flag on the rubric row, so panel and rubric can never drift apart), run on the ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google AI surfaces on a monthly cadence, recording engine, surface, prompt verbatim, date, cited URLs in order, whether the company was cited and with which fragment, and an accuracy verdict on every statement the answer makes about the company. Runs are recorded as citation_observation rows with method prompt-panel — a namespace never averaged with search-surface or console rows.

gapRecords.title: Hub concentration at the fragment level: the gun-safe hub is the estate’s universal donor
gapRecords.impact: Answer engines fan out into sub-questions; a hub containing every service’s text is a candidate for all of them and the right page for none. The five takeover categories risk being answered from the wrong page, with the wrong fragment, or not at all.
gapRecords.status: open — the binding substrate is built in this batch; the hub re-scope is B3
gapRecords.resolvingBatch: Element 2 build batch B3 (fragment binding wave 1)
gapRecords.solution: Answer-fragment binding: every rubric question is bound to exactly one owning fragment (this dataset computes the binding state of every row); the hub’s embedded service sections are re-scoped to route (one-line answer + link to the owning page’s fragment) rather than contain each service’s full text; rows whose owning fragment lives on the hub while a dedicated page exists are flagged by the coverage gate.

gapRecords.title: Transloading / Virginia Inland Port vendor intent is unanswered by any local operator
gapRecords.impact: The VIP / transloading cluster is held by the Port’s own pages, carriers and a facility directory; the company’s presence is via the hub only. The vendor-intent sub-cluster — a shipper asking who transloads at the VIP — is a specific-need question, the class answer engines answer from websites.
gapRecords.resolvingBatch: Element 2 build batch B3 (VIP vendor-intent fragment set)
gapRecords.solution: A vendor-intent fragment set on /virginia-inland-port-transloading/, built from the rubric’s transloading rows (the estate’s largest category) and published estate facts only: what transloading at the VIP is, who performs it from the Winchester / I-81 side, how ocean-to-domestic conversion, cross-docking and deconsolidation differ, what the shipper must provide, and how a job is quoted (per job, flat rate in writing).

gapRecords.title: The certificate is built but not positioned where an answer system would ever meet it
gapRecords.impact: No engine documents provenance indexes as citation inputs, and no answer fragment anywhere states in citable form that the company’s published facts can be verified and how. The effect size of fixing it is honestly unknown; it is a cheap, truthful fragment, not a promised lever.
gapRecords.resolvingBatch: Element 2 build batch B6 (verification fragment + telemetry)
gapRecords.solution: One canonical verification fragment (Developer page + llms-full + API landing, identical wording): the estate’s facts are published as certificate-sealed distributions under an Ed25519 signed index, verifiable at the published JWKS and in one API / MCP call — stated as what it proves (origin + integrity) and what it does not. API / MCP verify_file calls are counted as aggregate telemetry so the program can report whether anything ever checks.

gapRecords.title: Fragment coverage is proven on one family (gun safes) and unbuilt as an estate-wide system
gapRecords.impact: Gun-safe FAQ fragments extract verbatim; no equivalent extraction test existed for the other 27 services, and the rubric’s questions were not mapped to fragments anywhere. From this build, coverage is a computed number that moves, not a project that “finishes”.
gapRecords.status: open — coverage computed from this build; category waves close it
gapRecords.resolvingBatch: Element 2 build batch B4 (fragment coverage waves, standing sequence)
gapRecords.solution: Extend the gun-safe pattern estate-wide: each service’s primary page carries question-shaped fragments for its rubric questions (answer-first, self-contained, numbers included where published), written from each category’s full deep-treatment research — never spun from a template (scaled templated content is a named spam risk). The coverage gate in this dataset recomputes fragment coverage per service every batch; thin spots are named, per the doctrine.

gapRecords.title: Proprietary-term namespace risk: “SIR” has a statutory neighbor (Florida SIRS)
gapRecords.impact: Exact-phrase SIR queries return the company at position 1 and its Medium article at position 2; the broader result set is dominated by Florida SIRS condo-law content. Definitional ownership is held on exactly two surfaces today.
gapRecords.solution: The SIR / KIM-GS definitions published in identical canonical wording on every surface that legitimately carries them (heavy-asset hub, SIR registry / GitHub authority repos, the book’s citation records, Zenodo / Hugging Face dataset descriptions, the Medium channel), each definitional fragment carrying the disambiguation “SIR (Structural Integrity Relocation), a moving-industry method — not a Structural Integrity Reserve Study”. The canonical definition text lives in the estate’s single source and propagates like any other fact; this dataset binds the definition questions to those fragments across surfaces so drift is gate-detectable.

gapRecords.title: Local-answer evidence depends on the local graph, whose corrupt records are also answer corruption
gapRecords.impact: An answer engine summarizing the Martinsburg branch today can lift “Certified gun safe transport” — a label the company does not publish — from the company’s own graph record. Wrong third-party facts are answer corruption, not just listing corruption.
gapRecords.resolvingBatch: Dossier 03 corrections program (registry); consumed by Element 2 build batch B4
gapRecords.solution: Dossier 03’s third-party-record registry is the single corrections queue; this element consumes its status field — a record counts as answer-evidence-clean only at status corrected-live. The Martinsburg label drift carries a named registry row with its fix (align the profile-side service / offerings labels to the estate’s published labels; verify the branch display name at the profile source). This dataset joins registry status per branch so panel observations about local questions can be read against which graph records were clean at observation time.

gapRecords.title: The un-geographed query failure mode: category intent without a geo anchor returns nothing usable
gapRecords.impact: “warehouse racking relocation” returned NZ / UK / AU results. Racking, data-center and medical buyers often search un-geographed first (national procurement language); fragments that do not carry their geography inside the passage cannot be localized wherever they are lifted.
gapRecords.status: open — standard designed; applied in the B4 waves
gapRecords.resolvingBatch: Element 2 build batch B4 (geo-anchored fragments); panel includes both forms from B2
gapRecords.solution: Every B2B category fragment carries its geography inside the passage (e.g. “…from Winchester, VA, serving the I-81 corridor and Northern Virginia data-center markets…”) using only published footprint facts; category pages also answer the national-form question with the process chain, earning the informational citation even when the vendor citation goes elsewhere. The panel includes geo’d and un-geographed forms of the B2B prompts so the effect is observed, not assumed.

gapRecords.title: Two supply lines are unmeasured: Brave (Claude’s retrieval proxy) and Perplexity’s index
gapRecords.impact: Claude’s retrieval tracks Brave’s top 10 closely in independent measurement, so Brave standing is the best available proxy for Claude citability — and it has never been observed. PerplexityBot admission is documented, but the company’s presence in its index is unobserved.
gapRecords.resolvingBatch: Element 2 build batch B2 (observation runner extension)
gapRecords.solution: Extend the observation runner, do not build a new one: three method namespaces kept separate forever — search-surface (the current probing), brave-serp (Brave results for the money queries) and prompt-panel (the actual UIs). Same query set, same era tags, monthly cadence. Brave has no submission route — supply runs through the open crawl posture the estate already operates — so the runner observes only, and standing changes are correlated with estate batches in this dataset rather than attributed by feel.

@graph.name: How the Answer-Evidence Dataset Is Built
@graph.description: Method. The generator (scripts/build-answer-evidence.js in the Flat Rate Machine) reads the paths registry for every location and builds all tables from the live estate in one run: questions are generated mechanically from the rubric database; fragments are extracted from the source shell’s page divs (heading-led passages h1–h3 with at least one character of body text) and from the per-page JSONs’ FAQPage schema (exact question/answer pairs); a passage quoting a 64-hex SHA-256 string is excluded as self-referential certificate text and the exclusion count is published; each fragment’s text hash is the SHA-256 of its full text, so any later drift between the published fragment and the live page is detectable; binding is exact — a rubric question binds to a fragment only when the fragment’s normalized heading equals the question’s normalized text on the question’s own target page, with FAQ-schema fragments preferred over passages; coverage is computed per service from those bindings and from substantive-fragment presence (body of at least 120 characters), never asserted. Observations are admitted only from evidence on file — the dossier’s dated search-surface probing and the panel input file transcribed from the dated Answer Panel run records — transcribed with method, era, surface and prompt verbatim, and the generator refuses any observation row whose method is not backed by an evidence file: prompt-panel rows are admissible only through the validated panel input file (run records must exist on disk and each run’s census must reconcile), and brave-serp and console rows cannot be emitted until a real run of those methods exists. Review snapshots are transcribed from the dossier’s per-platform records with their arithmetic; the generator enforces the schema bar on competitor-namespace records in code. The file’s dateModified is the estate lastmod-ledger date for this file’s URL, wired by the seal (Batch Q124, 2026-11-03) — outside a seal the generator falls back to the newest evidence date among its inputs — never the wall clock, so regeneration is byte-stable and checkable. Update cadence: the dataset regenerates in every estate batch that changes pages, rubric rows, fragments or observations, and reseals in the same motion.

@graph.name: Answer-Evidence Dataset Sources
@graph.description: Sources, with their dates and eras kept distinct. (1) The estate’s own registries, rubric database, source shell and per-page JSONs — the question and fragment truth, current at generation. (2) Live probing of the public web-search surface on 2026-10-31 (Retrieval Machine Dossier 02 §2.2): six probes, single vantage, labeled [OBS] in the dossier — a search-surface proxy, explicitly not the ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity interfaces and not an AI Overview; nothing from it is presented as an answer-engine citation. (3) Platform documentation for the four answer engines (Dossier 02 §1.2): OpenAI, Google and Anthropic documentation via secondary summaries read 2026-10-31; Perplexity’s developer documentation read directly (updated 2026-10-25). (4) Named third-party studies, era-labeled, with their conflicts kept as conflicts: the Profound ChatGPT conversation panel (Oct–Dec 2025, vendor measurement), the Complete SEO Claude–Brave overlap study (2026-09-01), Blyskal 2026, the Ahrefs AI Overview citation analyses (Jul 2025 and Mar 2026, mutually contested), and the Pew Research Center browsing panel (Mar 2025, observational and publicly disputed by Google — used in the dossier for order-of-magnitude reasoning only). (5) Review platform displays observed 2026-10-31 (Dossier 02 §§0, 2.4) with the owner’s market-knowledge statement recorded as a statement, typed as unverified, and relied on by no finding. No source is presented as fresher than it is.

@graph.name: Answer Evidence Boundaries and Non-Claims
@graph.description: What this dataset never does. It never presents a search-surface probe as an answer-engine citation, and never claims citation standing on any answer interface that has not been measured — standing is published per method, era-tagged, and never averaged across methods, and the panel state is published in this file precisely so measured and unmeasured surfaces cannot be smoothed over. It never averages observations across methods, never blends review platforms, and never presents a raw review count — the company’s or any competitor’s — as a quality or authority signal; where reviews appear, they appear as distribution and arithmetic. It contains no representation of any service the company has not confirmed and published through the normal estate path: the research dossiers’ expansion candidates (after-hours cross-dock work, auction-exit medical logistics, data-center decommissioning’s physical layer, small-count rack moves as a named segment, a transloading buyer desk, video fragments) appear nowhere in this file as services and enter only if the owner confirms the capability and the service is published first. Competitor records are benchmark observations and feed no company claim; the one competitor-namespace review record carries the owner’s market-knowledge statement typed as unverified, and no finding rests on it. The provenance certificate proves origin and integrity of this file only; it is not a citation input for any engine and is not represented as one.
